parts.intro: You will hear a woman phoning a letting agency to ask about a flat she has seen advertised.

turns.text: Good afternoon, Brookside Lettings, Daniel speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about one of the flats on your website. The two-bedroom one... I think it was only listed this morning.
Sure. We've actually got a few two-bedroom places on the books at the moment. Do you have the address, or maybe the reference number?
Um, I don't have the reference, sorry. But it's on Ashgrove Street. Number twenty-two.
Ashgrove Street... let me just pull that up. Is that A-S-H-G-R-O-V-E?
That's right.
Okay, here it is. Twenty-two Ashgrove Street, the second-floor flat. Before I go through the details, can I take your name?
Yes, it's Laura Carrow.
And could you spell the surname for me?
C-A-R-R-O-W.
Thanks. So, Ms Carrow, what would you like to know?
Well, first of all, the rent. The website says seven hundred and sixty pounds a month. Is that still correct?
Ah, I'm afraid that figure's a little out of date. The landlord reviewed it last week, so it's now 785 a month.
Oh, I see. That's still within my budget... just about. And what about the deposit? Is it one month's rent?
Not quite. The deposit is five weeks' rent, which is the maximum we're allowed to ask for. It's held in a government-approved scheme, so you get it back at the end as long as there's no damage.
Okay. And when would it be free? I need to move before my course starts.
The current tenants leave at the end of August, and we need a few days to clean and check everything. So, it's available from the 1st of September.
That would be perfect, actually.
Can I ask about the bills? Are any of them included in the rent?

Water is included. Electricity and gas you'd pay yourself, and the same with the internet, so you'd choose your own provider. Council tax isn't included either, although as a full-time student you may not have to pay it.
Right. And is there anywhere to keep a bike? I cycle everywhere.
There's no garden, I'm afraid, and the hallway has to be kept clear for fire safety. But each flat has a lockable storage room in the basement, and that's big enough for a bicycle.
Oh, good. How far is it from the station? The listing said eight minutes' walk.
Hmm, honestly? I'd say that's a bit optimistic. Unless you walk really fast, it's more like twelve minutes. The bus stop is right outside the building, though.
That's fine. I'd love to see it. When could I come round?
Let me look at the diary... I could do Wednesday morning at ten?
Oh, Wednesday's no good, I'm working all day. Is there anything later in the week?
How about Thursday? I've got another viewing at four, so I could meet you after that... say, 5:30?
Thursday at 5:30 works for me.
Lovely. Now, if you decide to go ahead, we'll need to do a few checks. When you come to the viewing, could you bring your passport? We have to check everyone's right to rent.
Of course. Do you need anything else, like references?
We'll ask for a reference from your current landlord later on, but there's no need to bring anything else on Thursday. I'll email you a confirmation with the directions.
Thanks so much, Daniel.
You're welcome. See you on Thursday.

parts.intro: You will hear a volunteer coordinator giving an introductory talk to new volunteers at a hospital.

turns.text: Right, good morning, everyone, and welcome to Westfield Community Hospital. My name's Greg, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. I know some of you have come straight from work, so thank you. This morning I'll cover the basics of your role, and then we'll look at a plan of the ground floor so you can find your way around.

So, first things first. A lot of new volunteers assume they have to go to the security office at the start of each shift to pick up a badge. You don't. You collected your badge this morning, and it's yours to keep. You also don't need to report to the ward manager when you arrive; they're usually far too busy. What you must do, every single time, is sign in on the tablet at the volunteer desk in reception. That's how we know who's in the building if there's ever a fire alarm.

Now, hygiene. You won't be doing any clinical work, so you won't normally need gloves, and there's no monthly health check either, just the one you've already had. But hand hygiene is absolutely essential. You'll find gel dispensers at every ward door, and you must clean your hands every time you go into a ward and every time you come out. No exceptions.

People often ask me what the most valuable thing they can do on a ward is. Some of you will help at mealtimes, handing out trays, and some of you will walk patients down to their appointments, and that's all really helpful. But honestly, what makes the biggest difference is simply sitting and talking with patients who don't get many visitors. A twenty-minute chat can change someone's whole day.

Of course, patients will sometimes ask you about their condition or their medication. Even if you think you know the answer, please don't give any information yourself, not even general advice, and don't send them back to their relatives either. Just find one of the nurses and let them know the patient has a question.

And finally for this part, food. You're entitled to a free hot meal from the staff canteen, or a sandwich from the cafe if you prefer, any day of the week, provided you've done a shift of at least four hours. Just show your badge at the till.

Okay, if you look at the plan of the ground floor, you'll see we're standing in reception, here, with the main entrance behind us. In front of us is the main corridor, which runs from one end of the building to the other.

Your home base is the volunteer office. To get there, walk from reception up to the main corridor and turn left. It's on your right, the room immediately next to the pharmacy. That's where you'll find the rota and the kettle.
If patients or visitors want to buy a newspaper or a birthday card, send them to the shop. That's directly opposite the lifts, on the other side of the corridor.

We also have a quiet room, which is open to anyone who needs a peaceful space, whatever their faith. To find it, turn right into the main corridor and keep going right to the end. It's the very last room on your left.
Your volunteer lockers are in a small room between the cafe and reception. Please don't leave valuables in your coat on the wards; lock them away there.

And one more. Visitors often need to borrow a wheelchair, and they're kept in the wheelchair store. Go past the lifts, and it's the small room just before you reach the garden. If it's empty, call the porters on extension two-two-four.
Right, are there any questions before we take a walk round?

parts.intro: You will hear two trainees on a retail management course, Megan and Tom, talking to their supervisor, Carol, about a customer survey they ran.

turns.text: Come in, both of you. So, I've had a quick look at the figures from your customer survey. Shall we start with the response rate?
Yes. It was a lot lower than last year, wasn't it? We only got about two hundred replies.
We assumed at first it was because the survey was too long. But it's actually two questions shorter than last year's.

And we sent it on a Tuesday, same as last time, so the timing wasn't the problem either. What happened was that the link in the email didn't open properly on mobile phones. Most people tried it on their phones, saw a blank page and gave up.
Ah, that's frustrating, but it's a useful lesson. Now, what about the results themselves? Was there anything you didn't expect?

Well, we knew people would grumble about parking, because they always do. And the prices scored about the same as usual. What really surprised me was how many people went out of their way to praise the staff by name. We got over forty comments like that.
That's lovely to hear. Make sure that goes back to the store teams. Tom, you said you had an idea for next time?

Yes. I think sending another email reminder just annoys people, and a discount voucher would cost too much. So my suggestion is that staff simply ask customers at the till whether they'd be willing to answer three quick questions on a tablet.
I like that. It's cheap and it's immediate. Megan, you mentioned a prize draw as well.
Yes, entering everyone who replies into a draw for a gift card.

Hmm. Cost isn't really the issue, and there's nothing in company policy against it. My worry is that people rush through the questions just to enter the draw, so you get answers that don't really mean anything.
That's fair. So how should we structure the final report?
Well, the directors won't read twenty pages. Put the method in an appendix, and save the recommendations for the end. The very first page should be a one-page summary of what you found.
Now, let's go through the survey questions themselves, because I'd like you to improve them before next year. The first one, 'How did you hear about us?'
Nobody really needs that any more. Marketing gets that information from the loyalty card system, so I'd say we drop it altogether.
Agreed. What about 'Rate the cleanliness of the store'?
That one worked well. The answers were clear, and we can compare them with last year, so let's not touch it.
Fine. And 'Would you recommend us to a friend?'
The question itself is good, but at the moment it's the very first one, and people haven't thought about their visit yet. I think it would work better as the final question.
Yes, move it. Then there's 'How long did you wait?'

That's the one people misunderstood. Some thought it meant waiting at the till, others thought it meant waiting for help on the shop floor. We need to rewrite it so it's clear we mean the checkout queue.
Good. And finally, the comments box at the end.
Honestly, that gave us our best material. I wouldn't change anything about it.
Me neither. Right, send me the revised version by Friday and we'll book a meeting with the directors.

parts.intro: You will hear a lecture about methods used to restore damaged coral reefs.

turns.text: Good morning. Today we're moving from the biology of coral reefs to a more practical question: once a reef has been damaged, can we actually help it recover? And if so, how?

Let me start with why this matters. Coral reefs cover well under one percent of the ocean floor, and yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine species at some point in their life cycle. They also protect coastlines from storms and support fishing communities in more than a hundred countries.

Reefs face many threats, including pollution, overfishing and physical damage from boats and anchors. But by far the biggest driver of decline in recent decades has been bleaching. When the water becomes too warm for too long, corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which supply most of their food. The coral turns white, and if temperatures don't fall fairly quickly, it starves. So the main cause of bleaching is, quite simply, rising sea temperatures.

So, what can restoration do? The most widely used method is known as coral gardening. Divers collect small fragments from healthy corals, often pieces that have already broken off naturally, and grow them in underwater nurseries. In many projects, the fragments are hung from frames made of plastic pipe, which are shaped like trees, with branches at different heights. Because the fragments are off the sea floor, they're less likely to be buried by sand or eaten by predators. The nurseries do need regular maintenance, though. Every couple of weeks, divers have to clean the frames to remove algae, which would otherwise grow over the young corals and block out the light. After six months to a year, the corals are big enough to be attached to the damaged reef.

The second method is a more recent one called microfragmenting. Interestingly, it was discovered by accident. A researcher working with a slow-growing species broke a coral into very small pieces by mistake, and noticed a few weeks later that these tiny pieces had grown far faster than larger ones would have done. When several microfragments of the same coral are placed close together, they grow towards each other and fuse into a single colony. This is particularly valuable for the massive, boulder-shaped corals, which can otherwise take decades to reach a reasonable size.

Both of these methods, however, rely on cloning, so every new coral is genetically identical to its parent. That's a problem, because a population with low genetic diversity is less able to cope with change. This is where the third method, larval seeding, comes in. Many corals reproduce by releasing eggs and sperm into the water on just a few nights each year. Teams collect this spawn from the surface using floating nets, and then raise the larvae in tanks. When they're ready to settle, the larvae are given small ceramic tiles to attach to, and these tiles can then be wedged into the reef.

Finally, some damaged areas aren't suitable for any of these methods, because the reef has been broken into loose rubble. Young corals can't survive on a surface that keeps moving. So here, the first job is to stabilise the sea floor, and one approach is to fix the rubble in place with steel mesh coated in sand, which gives corals a firm base to grow on.

Now, I don't want to give you the impression that restoration is a solution in itself. Every one of these methods is limited by cost. Restoring a single hectare can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, which means the area we can treat is tiny compared with the scale of the damage. For this reason, many scientists now argue that restoration should focus on breeding corals with greater tolerance to heat, so that the reefs we rebuild have a better chance of surviving future warming. And of course, none of this replaces the need to reduce the emissions that are warming the oceans in the first place.

texts.title: Northgate Distribution: staying safe at work - a guide for new staff

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Northgate Distribution. Your safety, and the safety of the people around you, is our first priority. Please read this guide carefully before your first shift and keep it for reference. Your shift supervisor will go through the main points with you during your induction.

Protective clothing. Safety boots with steel toecaps must be worn in all warehouse areas. You will be given two pairs when you join, and replacements are free if your boots are damaged at work. In addition, high-visibility vests must be worn at all times in the loading bay, where lorries are constantly arriving and leaving. Vests are not required in the offices or the staff canteen.

Reporting accidents. If you are involved in an accident, however minor, you must report it to your shift supervisor before the end of your shift. This applies even if nobody is hurt, because small incidents often warn us about bigger risks. Every accident is then recorded in the accident book, which is kept in the first-aid room. Trained first-aiders wear a green badge, and a list of their names is displayed beside every exit.

Fire. When the alarm sounds, which is a continuous ringing bell, stop work immediately and leave the building by the nearest exit. Do not stop to collect personal belongings and do not use the lifts. The assembly point is beside the main gate, where your supervisor will check that everyone is present. Fire drills take place every three months and are not announced in advance.

Vehicles and equipment. Forklift trucks may only be driven by staff who hold a valid licence, and the licence must be renewed every three years. If you would like to train as a forklift driver, speak to your supervisor; the company pays for the course. When lifting boxes by hand, bend your knees rather than your back, and ask a colleague for help with anything over 20 kilograms. Never try to repair a machine yourself. If you notice a problem with any equipment, report it by completing the fault form on the staff intranet, and an engineer will be sent to inspect it.

texts.title: Northgate Distribution staff handbook: holidays and shift changes

paragraphs.text: This section explains how to arrange time off and how to change your shifts. It applies to all permanent employees. Temporary staff should refer to the agreement provided by their agency.

Annual leave. Full-time employees are entitled to 28 days' paid holiday a year, including public holidays. Part-time employees receive the same entitlement in proportion to the hours they work. The holiday year runs from 1 April to 31 March.

Requests should be made through the online system at least four weeks before the first day of leave. Requests are approved in the order in which they are received, so it pays to plan ahead, particularly for the summer months. Because December is our busiest period, leave cannot normally be taken in that month, except in cases of family emergency.

We encourage everyone to take their full entitlement. However, if you are unable to do so, up to five unused days may be carried over into the next holiday year. These must be used by the end of June, or they will be lost.

Shift swaps. We understand that personal commitments sometimes clash with the rota. You may swap a shift with a colleague who does the same job, provided that the swap is approved by a manager at least 48 hours in advance. Once it has been approved, it is your responsibility to make sure the change is shown on the rota, so that we always know who is on site. Swaps that have not been approved will be treated as an unauthorised absence.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than two hundred years, the lighthouse keeper was a familiar figure on the coasts of Europe and North America. Children read stories about them, painters placed them in front of crashing waves, and sailors depended on them every night of the year. Yet within a single working lifetime the occupation disappeared almost completely. In many countries, the last keepers handed over their keys in the final decades of the twentieth century, and today most of the world's lighthouses operate without a single person on site.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The working day of a keeper was shaped entirely by the light. Before electricity, lamps burned oil, and their wicks had to be trimmed several times a night so that the flame stayed bright and did not produce smoke. In the morning, the great glass lens was polished by hand, because even a thin film of soot could reduce the range of the beam. Many lights also turned by clockwork, which meant that someone had to wind a heavy weight back up the tower every few hours. In between these tasks, keepers kept a detailed log in which they noted the weather, the state of the sea and every vessel that passed. These records were later used by scientists studying climate and by investigators trying to understand shipwrecks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The experience of the job depended greatly on where a keeper was posted. At shore stations, keepers often lived with their families in cottages beside the tower, and their children attended local schools. Rock stations, built on isolated reefs or small islands, were very different. There, two or three men lived together in cramped rooms for several weeks at a time, while their families stayed on the mainland. They were supposed to be replaced on a fixed date, but the relief boat could only land in calm conditions, and in a stormy winter a keeper might wait a month or more before he was able to go home. Many filled the long hours with hobbies such as carving, painting or building model ships, and some became well known for the quality of their work.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Change came gradually, through a series of inventions. Electric lamps, introduced at many stations in the early twentieth century, removed the need to trim wicks. Automatic devices for changing bulbs followed, so that a failed bulb could be replaced without human hands. One of the most important developments was a valve, designed by a Swedish engineer, that responded to daylight and switched a gas-powered light off at dawn and on again at dusk. Because the light now burned only when it was needed, a single supply of gas could last for many months, and some smaller lights could be left entirely alone. Later, radio links allowed engineers on the mainland to check a light's condition from many kilometres away.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Despite these advances, many authorities moved slowly. Converting a large station was expensive, and some engineers doubted whether machines could be trusted on the most exposed rocks, where salt water and storms damaged everything. Keepers themselves argued that they did far more than tend a lamp. Because they watched the sea constantly, they were often the first to see a vessel in difficulty, and over the years they had raised the alarm for many crews and helped to rescue people from the water. They also sent regular weather observations, which were valued by forecasters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the end, however, the economic case proved impossible to resist. Satellite navigation meant that ships relied less on lights, and the cost of employing staff at remote stations kept rising. The final keepers left their posts with mixed feelings. Some were relieved to give up a hard and lonely life, but many felt that something valuable was being lost. A number of them stayed on as part-time attendants, visiting the automated lights regularly to carry out maintenance. Meanwhile, the empty cottages were sold or rented out, and many are now holiday homes whose guests pay to experience the isolation that the keepers once endured.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Interest in the keepers has, if anything, grown since they left. Several towers have become museums, and in some places volunteers act as guides during the summer months, explaining how the stations once worked. Historians have also realised that the generation who remember the job is getting older. Oral history projects have therefore recorded long interviews with former keepers and their families, preserving details that were never written down, from the recipes cooked on rock stations to the songs that were sung to pass the time. Thanks to this work, a way of life that has vanished from our coasts will not vanish from our memory.

tasks.prompt: You live in a rented flat. For the past two months, building work on the flat next to yours has been causing a lot of noise. Write a letter to the property manager. In your letter, describe the noise and when it happens, explain how it is affecting you, and say what you would like the property manager to do. Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows: Dear Sir or Madam,

bullets: describe the noise and when it happens
explain how it is affecting you
say what you would like the property manager to do

key_features: Formal tone throughout; clear purpose stated in the first lines (complaint about noise from building work).
Bullet 1: specific description of the noise (drilling, hammering) and times/days, including any work outside permitted hours.
Bullet 2: concrete effects (sleep, working from home, health, children), not just 'it is annoying'.
Bullet 3: a realistic, specific request (limit working hours, advance notice, a timetable, a rent reduction) and a deadline or follow-up.
Appropriate formal close (Yours faithfully) and full name; logical paragraphs; at least 150 words.

model_answer.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing as the tenant of Flat 4B to complain about the noise caused by the renovation of Flat 4C, which has now continued for almost two months.

The work involves heavy drilling and hammering through the shared wall, and on most days it begins at around 7 am, well before the 8 am start time stated in the building rules. On several occasions the noise has also continued into the evening and even on Sundays.

This is having a serious effect on me. I work night shifts at a hospital three times a week, so I need to sleep during the morning, which has become almost impossible. As a result, I have been exhausted at work and have had to take two days of unpaid leave.

I would therefore be grateful if you could remind the contractors of the permitted working hours and ask them to avoid the noisiest work before 10 am. I would also appreciate a timetable showing when the work is expected to finish. If the disturbance continues, I would like to discuss a temporary reduction in my rent.

I look forward to hearing from you within the next week.

Yours faithfully,
Samira Haque

tasks.prompt: Some people believe that all secondary school students should have compulsory cooking lessons, so that they learn to prepare healthy meals. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
key_features: A clear position (agree, disagree or partly agree) stated in the introduction and kept consistent to the conclusion.
Main ideas such as health and obesity, independence and saving money, family and cultural knowledge, against pressure on the timetable and the cost of kitchens and teachers.
Each main idea developed with explanation and a relevant example.
Counter-argument acknowledged and answered if the writer agrees (or the reverse).
Paragraphing, linking and a range of vocabulary (nutrition, processed food, curriculum, life skills); at least 250 words.

model_answer.text:
In many countries, young people are leaving school able to solve equations but unable to cook a simple meal. For this reason, some argue that cooking should become a compulsory subject in secondary schools. I largely agree with this view, although the lessons need to be practical and carefully planned.

The strongest argument for compulsory cooking lessons concerns health. Teenagers increasingly rely on fast food and ready meals, which are often high in salt, sugar and fat, and this contributes to rising rates of obesity and diabetes. A student who knows how to prepare a quick vegetable curry or a simple pasta dish has a real alternative to takeaway food. Moreover, cooking lessons naturally teach nutrition, so students would understand why certain foods are better for them rather than simply being told so.

Cooking is also a vital life skill with financial benefits. Students who leave home for university or work often spend a large part of their income on convenience food. Being able to plan meals and cook in bulk can save a considerable amount of money, and it gives young people a sense of independence and confidence.

Critics point out that the school timetable is already crowded and that equipping kitchens is expensive. These concerns are valid, but cooking does not need to replace core subjects; even one lesson a week for two years would make a difference, and schools could share facilities or use simple equipment.

In conclusion, I believe the benefits of compulsory cooking lessons for students' health, finances and independence clearly outweigh the practical difficulties, provided the lessons focus on simple, affordable and healthy meals.
